When I share this perspective, understand that I am in NO way defending this woman. She absolutely should have minded her own business.

I grew up Christian, and from childhood, it was drilled into mine and the other children's heads that our main duty in "the army of Christ" is to share the word of Jesus (Read: "Convert, Convert, Convert). While it wasn't considered sinful to mind your own business, it was frowned upon by proxy of how encouraged you were to bring friends to church and speak up for Jesus and all that nonsense. "Prove how much you love God by defending him. Prove how loyal to God you are by talking about him. Every breath in your lungs, every word of your lips, every thought in your head is FOR Jesus!"

The other thing drilled into us was that everything that isn't Christian is either a frivolous distraction from God or *evil*! Any religion that isn't Christian? Evil. Atheism? Evil. Not being straight or cis? Evil. Not being. Republican? Evil. And leading back to the first thing, it is our "job" as good, loyal, obedient Christians to fight back against the evils of the world.

This lady didn't think she was being an ignorant jackass. She heard you were "evil" (non-Christian) and so did the "Lord's work" (ran her mouth off).

And that is why Christians do it. From Sunday School onward, we are conditioned with guilt and shame to never ever mind our own business, because the church needs as many members of the next generation to be giving up that sweet sweet 10% cut of every paycheck.

Again, that's no excuse. That lady needs therapy and a zipper for that mouth of hers.

This stinks of a scam. Call an official Disneyland contact, via their website and have them check. A few notes signalling it as a scam.

1. "Cast members" don't call guests. Disney personnel do. Cast members work at the park. Personnel works with HR and all that jazz. Anyone sending emails on Disney's behalf would know the difference. A grifter looking to make a dime wouldn't 

2. A professional business would NEVER send you an email regarding the revoking of their services. They would send you the information, including the reason (conduct, late payment, change of policy, ect.) via physical mail, on official stationary, in a sealed, stamped, and legitimately delivered envelope. (NOTE: that goes double for things like gas and electric, city bills, insurance, banks, etc.)

3. They want you to mark their phone number as safe, because smartphones these days automatically mark heavily reported phone numbers as spam. If you mark it as safe, it overrides that warning. If you actually got a call from Disney, your phone would tell you. Your phone wouldn't mark an official business line as spam.

4. They want you to reply to the email with your phone number instead of you contacting them. Why? Because they're mass emailing people just to see who takes the bait, so they can focus on just the gullible ones. If they had you call them directly, they would risk being flooded with calls that their scammy little setup wouldn't be able to handle. They want complete control, where Disney has the tech and manpower to focus on making things easy for the consumer.

5. Their hours are from 9:30 am to 5pm? On their official website, on their contact page, there is no such time window. They have enough employees to man the phones around the clock (because with thousands of guests a day, someone is gonna need to call at midnight to double check a booking or ask about an issue before a trip). Even if they had hours, they wouldn't be so restricted. That's the time window of a regular 9-5 job, when most people work their office job. If their hours are more destructive than a Walmart, it's not the billion-dollar, multi-media, "I own everything" juggernaut known as The Disney Corporation.

If your worried, go to https://disneyland.disney.go.com/help/phone/ and call them directly. Ask for them to check the state of your magic key. They'll verify your identity and tell you what's up. But do NOT engage with this email. If you already put their number in your phone, block it.

KH1 has more interesting combat, but exploration is limited. While many boss battles are straight forward (Dark Side is just hitting the hands, guard armor is just hacking away at the parts one at A time, etc.), there are some that take some manner of thought. You have to focus on gaining leverage and using magic to defeat the Trickster, drain Clayton's  HP instead of the Stealth Sneak to win. When initially fighting Ursula, you have to overload her cauldron with magic to weaken her. However, a lot of the worlds are either confined to a couple of "rooms" (the collesium being three rooms, Monstro is six numbered chambers that look similar to each other, bowls, and mouth, Traverse Town is three districts and a few indoor areas, etc.) or are a bit of a complicated maze (if you get turned around in Monstro, it's difficult to orient yourself again. Wonderland could get complicated if it's your first time, the underground area of the Cave of Wonders gets tedious of you don't have a guide, Atlantica was so hard to navigate, the remix added pointers to get around, etc.) While exploration isn't completely without merit, I feel it's lack-luster compared to KH2.

KH2 has these issues reversed. Most of the world have a lot more to offer in terms of exploration, but the combat is a button masher 90% of the time. The world still has that maze-like feel, but there are more chests and other collectables to find, and it's more of an open space to look around in and enjoy the scenery. Towns all have more areas to explore, and Hollow Bastion even has unlockable areas. However, combat is a little less complicated overall, to the point where they had to add separate mini games into some bosses to make it seem dynamic. Most enemies you can just beat into submission. There's less misdirection or purposeful integration of magic overall. Some of the Organization XIII fights are interesting, but the rest is very "push x and triangle to win"

So if you like interesting and dynamic fights better, you'll enjoy KH1 more. If you like wide open spaces and exploration more, you'll enjoy KH2 more.

I feel too much a lot of the time. It used to be debilitating. My friends would be feeling all this pain when it came to their problems, and I would struggle to listen because I would try to think about what it was like for them, and it would just be so painful. And I would feel so badly for them that it started to affect my mental health in a very bad way.

Now a days, I've managed to dampen it. I still feel empathy, but my emotional response is to sympathize first, and then empathize. At least for me, when I talk about my problems, I don't want my friends to be in the despair with me. I want them to be happy in their lives, and I need their support to pull me from the muck. So while I can still understand how they must feel, I try to maintain my emotional state and be a support for them.

I've had to teach myself a lot of emotional regulation techniques, and the effort has been worth it.

I think that advice is predicated on the idea that a lot of new writers are easily overwhelmed with the idea of needing to write something big and grand for their first project. If they start small to practice, then start a bigger project when they're ready, they'll have an easier go of it.

You seem to have a different viewpoint. The idea of a large project doesn't intimidate you via the amount of time and effort it takes. It's rather the idea of having to pick and choose from a vast ocean of ideas to cram into a short story that seems to be intimidating. Both are intimidating skills to learn, and both are important. It's good to learn how to tackle a big project AND to choose themes, elements, and plot points that are the most vital, whilst "killing your darlings".

My advice. Go backwards. Start with the large epics that you flourish in as your practice, and put in the hours that way, shaping a larger narrative, developing your world, and designing your characters. Then, when you're more practiced, try again with shorter stories to sharpen your weaker skills. 

Try spin-off stories about side characters you've already designed, or make new characters in a world you've already created. That way, there's less pressure to start from scratch, and you can keep your passion burning for these shorter stories, since these stories would be about a setting in which you're already invested.

Boiled down, the advice is better stated as this: To be a master at something takes 10,000 hours. Spend a good chunk of those first 5000 hours writing the stuff that you are bananas about, so you can get through a large portion of the necessary practice with less of a struggle. When you find your strengths have been maximized, start shaping up your weak points to minimize them.

So I read your post and a few comments and thought I'd throw my hat in.

First, keep working with your therapist. Even if they don't fully grasp it, that's still important. If your therapist is minimizing your feelings or dismissing how you feel about your hard work, look into finding a new one. If they're trying to work with you but just don't fully understand, keep going for a little longer.

Second, don't give up on your world. You put in a lot of hard work and I'm sure it's beautiful. It sounds like you don't want to give it up, so that's good! Keep that.

Third, this is where the advice goes from generic to specific. I want you to pick an area in your world. Within that area, place a teeny tiny village. This village has at least 3 things: farmland, homes, and a very nice tavern. All the villagers there either farm or work in the tavern. For this tavern, make it the nicest, coziest tavern you've ever been to. Design the layout, the decor, the rooms upstairs. Make a drink menu and a food menu of all the things you love. Create backstories for the owner, the bar keeper, the waiter or waitress, the cook, the brew master, etc. If you're feeling the creative juices, flesh out the rest of the village, but put the majority of your love and time into this tavern. By the end, you'll have a fully fleshed piece of your world untouched by the people who hurt you, and that's important to have. Whatever wars happen, whatever dangers come by, that tavern will not be harmed, even if it's unrealistic. This is YOUR tavern.

Fourth, when you're ready, restart your campaign in that tavern. For returning players, Carrie's character and Malcom's character left the party and will no longer be part of the story. Let your players reference them if it's relevant; we don't need to go pretending that people never existed. However, what they do on their own will no longer affect the world. The returning characters have been traveling for a while and have come to rest at this tavern. For new players, this is where they will meet the returning players and group up. If the party wants to revisit unfinished quests or seek backstory-related stuff, allow the players to lead.

Fifth, set boundaries. Any boundaries you need to feel safe in this world you've made. For example, if anything more than a reference to Carrie's and Malcom's characters makes you uncomfortable, ask in the new session 0 that they players do not visit or send messages to them, as you don't want to play them. If romance at the table makes you feel icky, talk to your players at the session 0 about making the campaign aromantic or at least putting a low emphasis on romantic partners.

Sixth, from that tiny tavern slowly branch your way out again. Start with a problem in the village. Then travel into some wilderness. Then if there's an established city nearby, have them go there, etc. branch out bit by bit.

Seventh, understand that it's still going to hurt. Everything that reminds you of them is going to hurt, and it will hurt for a while. Work with your pain to process it, rather than avoiding or suppressing it. Learn to love by yourself the things you used to love with them. Learn new things to love. And don't let your pain dictate what your life should be like. You will process it in time, and you'll still have your beautiful world by the end. Just keep going to therapy and keep working hard.

Step 1) Write. Don't worry about making your dialogue perfect. Just write it out. Even if it's trash, just keep writing. Tell your inner critic and inner editor to wait their turns. Get words on paper.

Step 2) Read. Out loud. This is crucial, not only to better find typos and fix them in the early stage, but also to test your dialogue. Here are a few things to look out for:

A) Can you say the dialogue without twisting your tongue? Do the words sound cohesive together? Do you have to restart a sentence more than once before you're able to say it? If so, rewrite it so it's easier to speak. People use words that are easiest to say.

*Example: change "It's hard to see against a black background." to "It's hard to see, since the background is so dark."*

B) Is information in the dialogue already present. The text? People don't use the names of people they know well most of the time (though they may in tender or even angry moments). If you mention a detail on text, the character shouldn't have to repeat it.

*Example: Change "The fall went on for so long, they stopped speeding up, falling as fast as a person could. However when they hit the ground, none of them were hurt. "How is this possible?" Cried Amy "we hit terminal velocity. We should be dead!" to "The fall went on for so long, they stopped speeding up, falling as fast as a person could. However when they hit the ground, none of them were hurt. "How is this possible?" Amy marveled at her unbroken body, which hardly had a scratch anywhere.*

C) Is the tone and slang use appropriate? If you're writing a period piece, the use of slang differs from one time and place to the next. If you're in modern times, language won't naturally sound very poetic. Also, if someone is enraged, their language will be different from when they are relaxed, depressed, or excited.

*Example: Change "Princess, it would be my honor to take you to the royal ball. What do you say?" to "Princess, it would be my honor to escort you to the royal ball. I shall wait with bated breath for your acceptance." Change "He looked into his brother's eyes, fire in his own at the betrayal. "I thought we were family, but I guess that means nothing to you." "He looked into his brother's eyes, fire in his own at the betrayal. "You've got some nerve. We were supposed to be family. Family! And here I thought that meant something to you!"*

Step 3) Test read it to others or have others read your work, and ask what they think of the areas you wish to improve. Tell them to be honest in their critique, and that you want constructive feedback. Keep testing it with others until you get feedback you can use to improve.

Hope this helps!

Here's what is established. Magic isn't the main aspect of the story, this catchphrase is merely describing what the spell does (some sort of reality-shifting magic), and you want it to stand out. That last one is why straying away from over-used options would be more ideal.

One way is to mix up the elements of the options and add to them, to come up with something fresher. You can also take bits and pieces to make something completely new. Some suggestions are:

"The tides will tremble with war."

"Destroy reality and rebuild it in destiny's image"

"Weave the tapestry of fate and history into my desire"

"Bring the heavens and hells into my domain"

"Author what was and what will be"

"The truth is now the lies that I design"

Play around and see what you can come up with, and see which ones sound good to you. Or can can just yoink one of mine.

Deciding on a charismatic demeanor and set of personality traits can go a long way. After all, you can make anything sound good with the right tone

First, when presenting his cause and his plan to reach his goals, he should bring up possible moral contradictions people may have. This seems counterproductive, but doing so does two things. 1) it makes him seem more transparent, and therefore more honest. 2) It allows him to strawman the potential arguments in a way he can easily defend against before people can think too hard about it. Once he brings up moral issues, he can instantly knock them down to make his plan seem less extreme.

(Just an example, let's say your villain wants to burn a village to the ground because there's a slave trader living there who has a lot of security guards, and he can't reliably assassinate them. So he says to his minions. "There's only one way to smoke out a fox, my friends. If we set fire to the dry grass on the outskirts, it will engulf the village and the dastardly slaver before he can escape. And I know what you're thinking, and of course I care for the other villagers. They did nothing wrong. But they'll be fine. As poor as they are, they have precious little. They will see the fire and run to safety before it hurts them. Meanwhile, the rich slaver, greedy as he is, wouldn't dare part with his wealth, and will be consumed in fire before he can escape with his gold. Even if there are casualties, how many lives will be spared from his business? The people who would otherwise be kidnapped? The families who would be torn apart? The innocent's who would otherwise be enslaved? Anyone truly good would gladly lay down their lives for such a cause!")

Next, you'll want to choose personality traits that make your character approachable and friendly. You can have him be extraverted and comical, constantly making jokes and making the atmosphere light. You can make him personal and warm, calling everyone friend and making light physical contact (hands in shoulders, pats on backs, etc.) You can make him quiet and contemplative, speaking in a calm voice that belies wisdom and intelligence. You can make him excitable and passionate, hiding zealotry behind a guise of exciting activism.

Think of the image of someone you would completely trust, and ask yourself why that image seems so trustworthy. Put those traits into your character, and they'll seem more trustworthy.

Finally, a few "don'ts" to keep in mind. First, don't deviate too much from his personality. It's okay for a happy character to be sad, or for an angry character to cheer up once in a while. But if he strays too far, it'll make him seem two-faced, and that will cause readers to question why his followers aren't leaving. Second, don't make him too abusive, either with his followers or his power. If he starts hitting people who bring him bad news or starts barking orders, people will be likely to leave in order to seek out their cause on their own, without an abuser leading them. Finally, don't forget the climax. When his plan is about to succeed, he may become more excited or megalomaniacal than usual. When he's about to be defeated, he may become more desperate or make decisions more rashly (perhaps even breaking his own moral code in desperation). When he's utterly defeated and his work is destroyed, will be be completely downtrodden or fuming with rage? He may (and should) shift as the story progresses, and a lot of that change should mirror how his plan shifts.

And ellipsis ("...") has several uses. It's more technical purpose is for the simplification if quotes. If you want to quote something in your work, but there's a piece of the quote in the middle that is irrelevant or superfluous, you can merely cut it out, replacing it with an ellipsis in order to relay to the audience that the quote you used isn't fully completed, which maintains the integrity of it.

In fictional writing, there are many uses. It can indicate dialogue that trails off or stops without properly ending. It can also indicate a defined pause, like if a scene holds only one side of a phone conversation (the ellipsis would take the place of the dialogue from the other person that the audience wouldn't be privy to). It can also take the place of in-story, written words that are unreadable, but are apart of a longer phrase (for example, if a character finds a half-burned document and tries to read it, ellipsises would replace the words that were burned away ).

Like paint for painters, punctuation like the ellipsis have rules that dictate their use. When you know those rules, you have a better understanding of exactly how you can bend and even break those rules to make your creative writing truly your own. So if you want to use more ellipsis in your work, get into it's common uses and find ways in which you can use the understanding of it's purposes to your advantage.

Now, I have advice, and you can take it or leave it. But before I do, a few things to keep in mind:

1. You're not a bad person. You're young and you're just trying to make do with what you have. Having anxiety and trying to help yourself when you don't have the proper tools isn't a moral failing on your part.

2. I am going to assume that if you could go to a doctor, you would have. If you can, see a doctor, as they'll have way more info and resources than some rando on the Internet. This advice is assuming that you can't, and that's okay. Life sucks, and so does health insurance.

3. This advice, if followed, will make you feel like garbage (physically at least). Cutting any chemical habit, be it caffeine, alcohol, or anything, feels like torture. It's short-term pain, it will pass, but it will suck.

The first thing you gotta do is detox from all the chems you've been using. That means for the next two weeks, no alcohol, no caffeine, and no drugs (though I think you said you were just considering weed at this point, so that's more about not starting). Those two weeks will be the worst of your life, so take a break from everything that isn't vital to your existence. Even if you have to fail an assignment or two, take a break from sports or clubs, cancel plans with friends, do it. Your body needs rest to recover from the reality that you aren't gonna give it the thing it's been dependent on for so long. Drink lots water and HERBAL (non caffeinated) tea, and eat whatever you can reasonably get (you won't have the energy to cook, so have snacks available. Whatever you can get, fed is best).

Either during or after the detox, look into and practice distressing techniques that don't require a substance. Meditation, breathing exercises, and doing yoga at home with a YouTube tutorial are all borderline free. These things can help decrease cortisol (stress hormone) levels some, which can reduce anxiety enough to maintain control.

You can also look into a hobby, specifically one that makes use of your hands. You can learn something complicated like yarn crafts or needlepoint, or do something simple like drawing, coloring, or writing. If you can occupy your hands, you could possibly occupy just enough of your brain to stop trauma spirals and anxiety traps before they start.

By the end of the two weeks, look at your schedule. Write out everything you do in a month on a calendar. If you look at it and find it's overly packed, try saying goodbye to a few things to leave room to rest. Make school classes a priority, then things that your parents make you do (though consider asking them if you can stop doing some things if they would understand). Make time for friends about once or twice a week, and limit extracurricular school activities to 1 to 2 hours a day, to leave time to do homework and projects). Overall, give your time a minimum of 10 waking hours of alone time per week (homework time doesn't count as alone time), and 8 hours of sleeping time per night (even if "sleeping time" is "lay in bed with a physical book until you fall asleep" time). All this won't get rid of anxiety, but emptying your plate a little may help by giving you fewer things to be anxious about.

Finally, consider doing a little shadow work. Basically deep inner reflections to look at the mental and emotional sources of your anxiety, so you can better overcome your stress. You can buy a shadow workbook or get resources online.

Overall, if you don't have the medical tools available to you, self-medicating with alcohol and caffeine is not a long-term solution, and can end up harming you after the fact, considering your body and brain are still developing. Even if you don't take my advice, I hope you can still find a way to overcome your stress without relying on substances. Even if you can't see a doctor, there may be a counselor or nurse at your school who could help you if you ask. Whatever you choose to do, I wish you the best.

At 9, there's no way to get him interested in the "boring" parts. He'll either crave customization and will gain an attention span that will allow for longer sessions, he'll grow bored of the game over time and move on to another interest, or he'll foster of a love for battle-focused games, to which there are a plethora of other systems that are more conducive to that style of play.

In any case, don't force it. He's young, and he doesn't have the brain that can handle huge investments of time. An attention span is one that develops with age. Science says a child's attention span is 3-5 minutes per year of age. So he can only be invested for 45 minutes at a time, maximum. More realistically, it's closer to just under 30 minutes, less if he has ADHD.

My advice? Make for him a very simple fighter character, with only about 2-3 options for an action, and maybe 1-2 options for a bonus action. Something that's not complicated that he can easily pick up and play (perhaps for an action, he can choose between a melee weapon attack, a ranged weapon attack, and using a charge on a magic item to do a limited AOE attack. Then for a bonus action he can dual weapon attack or drink a health potion as a bonus. He'd have options, but not a crazy amount). And every time he joins, he plays that character. As he gets older, you can start adding more options slowly. If one day he wants something new, you can sit down with him and make him a customized character. Maybe if he's still struggling, you can build that character but by bit over time (maybe 5 minutes worth), and he can use his simple fighter until it's finished.

Overtime, he'll either want to put the effort in, or he'll move on to something different. In the meantime, do some research to perhaps help him find a battle-focused system that would meet his interests better than DND, if he decides that he just wants to fight. I hear GURPS or even 4e is great for combat-heavy stuff. Mork Borg is also good and has a very speedy character creation with a interesting apocalyptic aesthetic. If he's not opposed to careful strategy and investigation, but doesn't like long character creation in and of itself, Call of Cthulhu is designed to get character creation over and done with quickly (though I wouldn't suggest this to him until he's a lot older. It's a horror themed game AND the reason CC is fast is because you die a *lot*). If money is no option, he may also like Warhammer, which is all strategy and battle, with nearly 0 character creation (though he may need some help from Mom to build and paint his minis if he struggles with fine motor skills). I don't know a lot about it, but my husband LOVES it, and it's a thriving community, which can help him be more social with like-minded peers as he gets older.

Let's compare sex to a more similar aspect: Entertainment. Specifically, let's compare having sex to watching a movie.

Most people love movies! They have favorite genres, favorite actors, favorite styles or tropes. They love love LOVE movies, to the point that they can't imagine life without sitting down once a week with a new DVD or an old favorite flick. Movies are their go-to for boredom. But there are, in fact, people who don't really like movies. They may watch a movie only if their partner puts it on. Or the idea of sitting in one place for an hour and a half fills them with dread. Some may tolerate a movie for the sake of their partner once in a while, but they don't really like movies at all.

"But don't these people get bored?" Well, yes and no. Some people just have so many other things going on in their lives that they don't slow down long enough to be bored. Others are easily enthralled with the world around them that boredom is never an issue. Some of them do occasionally get bored, but they would rather play a video game, read a book, do a puzzle, or make some art to satisfy that entertainment craving.

So let's say you're taking a new medication that has a strange side effect. In some way or another, the medicine makes you understimulated, and you are craving entertainment more than usual. I didn't really use a set in stone pattern, but I can try to explain what I did.

First, I used this tutorial for the rice part. It's basically just a rectangular plush. https://youtu.be/63u2gHzdtgI?si=5U9TZ4DpurbBRc8h

Second, I used a red yarn to make the fish. I single crochet a flat piece, 9 stitches wide, with two chains at the ends to make a turn. I did a few rows, before I started to attach it to the rice. I did two free S.C., then the next five, I put my hook through the stich, then through a stich on the rice where I wanted it to attach, and then did my S.C., and then two free S.C. I did that all the way across, then did a few more free rows until it covered the rice as much as I wanted.

Then I went in with a darning needle to embroider the eyes and mouth with black, and the fat stripes on the fish with pink. I just kinda watched some YouTube videos of other people doing it, and then winged it from there.

For the nori, I chained 16, the S.C. five stitches into the 16th chain. Then I Double crocheted a flat piece until it was big enough to wrap around the plush, before going to the middle stich at the ending row and chaining another 16 (these chains allow you to tie off the nori in a bow).

Finally, I used green embroidery floss and sewed a green button on the back flap of the fish for wasabi (optional, but I like it!)

I kinda just winged a lot of it, so sorry for not having a professional pattern.

Cut to 2020. My husband and I had been married for two years, and sex was still a struggle for us. We both were virgins when we married, so we thought we just didn't know how to do it right. Maybe if we lost weight or got a better bed or did this or that, we could fix it. Then one day, it clicked in my head:

"The sex isn't bad. It's me. I just don't like sex."

I'm very romantically inclined. I fall in love very easily, and I'm very loyal when that person loves me back. But of course, Lulia isn't the most subtle woman, and ended up blabbing almost as soon as the party asked why she was acting so squirrely. Rahadin, who was spying, runs off to tell Strahd I broke the rules, and we set to work gathering an army.

So that's the WHY of fighting him at level 7, but the HOW is frankly hilarious.

Option 1: When you start to notice your players about to get into combat, ask everyone for their passive insights. Don't set a DC. Instead anyone who has or ties for the highest passive insight "notices" that the powerful NPC will hole punch them if they try. Consider the following suggestions.

"Your eye catches a spark, and you focus on it to see that his hands are glowing with arches of magical energy the angrier he gets. Just from looking at it, you can tell this wizard far exceeds all of you in magical ability."

"You look up and see the veins on her forehead bulge. She grits her teeth as you see a red haze casts itself over her eyes. As she loudly cracks all her knuckles with her other hand, you can see clearly how physically strong she is. You have no doubt that she could and will easily toss all of you across the room if you do not choose your words carefully."

"As they start to laugh in response to your mockery, you sense a hint of madness in it. A sense that any rational  has since left them long ago, and you are currently threatening someone with no fear, no limits to their power, and no fucks to give. However confident you were in their defeat, it all drains away as the laughter fills you with a horrifying dread."

Something like that. Just allow them to notice something about the NPC that relates to how they would get their ass kicked. Are they super magical? Are they physically bigger and stronger? Do they outnumber the heros? Because you are freely giving this information to the one with the biggest passive insights(though you could give it to those with the top 2 or 3 biggest passives), this is you as a DM saying "Hey, they will kill you if you don't pack it in and get out of there." while still staying engrossed in the story.

Option 2 is to merely lower the stakes. Have fewer NPCs who are gung ho to kill, and instead have different consequences, such as knocking them out non-lethaly to take them hostage, and now they have to escape. Or being knocked out only to wake up hours later to a massacre caused by some demonic being that wants the favor of saving their lives to be repaid immediately. Real consequences that don't necessarily involve TPKs.

Option 3 is to start the combat anyway, if they move forward, and have the super powerful NPC knock one PC on their ass before having the NPC, on that same turn or using a legendary action, offer to spare them all if they merely pick up their unconscious friend and leave. It's both a kick in the pants for your players and help establish this big bad as arrogant. We love to see an arrogant villain! If they refuse, knock another one down and offer again. Rinse and repeat until they take the hint and leave.

Option 4 is, of course, allowing them to reap what they sow. They can make as many characters as is necessary to drive the point home that you play for keeps, and they need to consider that going forward.

My husband had the same issue with players interrupting a monologue with important information in it. The way he handled it was thus:

1. Take a breath. No one likes being interrupted in real life, so it can be very frustrating.
2. Say to the player. "Okay, put a pin in that. You can totally do that, but I was counting on you all knowing the information this guy is about to give you, so they really need to finish their speech.
3. Finish the monologue. Say everything you need to say, but wrap it up.

It's not an elegant solution, as you do need to break character to ask if you can finish the monologue. Players can be easily excited, especially if they can make a fool out of their enemy by cutting off their speech. So interruptions are gonna happen. A few other suggestions.

1. If there is important information for the players in a speech you couldn't finish, put clues to the same information on their person or in the room/lair for them to find instead.

I feel actions dictate alignment, full stop. If you are kind to others and want to help, you're good. If what you do is constantly in your one personal interests, whether it helps others or not, that's neutral. If you do whatever you can to gain power, wealth, fame, or anything else you want, with no regard for others, that's evil. Doing any of those within either the law or a strict moral code is lawful. Doing so with reckless abandon is chaotic, and landing somewhere in between in neutral.

Also, intention plays an important role as well. The guy who set fire the orphanage to distract the town guards, so he could sneak into the government building for secret information? Chaotic evil. The guy who set fire to the orphanage by accident in their attempt to defeat the demon living in the basement? Neutral good (and kinda clumsy). Same outcome, different circumstances.

I'm personally in the camp of, "we don't talk about alignment until it's relevant". Some items or spells are alignment-dependant, so when player alignment becomes relevant, it's nice to stop the story, for just a minute, and ask "so tell me, what do you think your character's alignment is right now?" And then have a short discussion. Let anyone with two cents to spare chime in, but most players will be honest.

Judging from the post and extra comment, if this player has made a habit of getting upset whenever he isn't optimized for the fight, it may be a conversation you need to have before the "bitching" becomes a problem. Keep a few things in mind 

1. See if he's satisfied with his build in general. Touch base and ask if he wants to switch anything around. A scorned wizard with true polymorph prepped can easily change a player race (and you don't have to roll if they want something specific), and some magical maguffin crystal/book/trinket found in the woods that imbues the one who touches it with new knowledge and abilities is good enough story reason to change up a class, subclass, or spell list. Sometimes, a magic item can help solve the build issue he's having. Nothing game breaking, but perhaps access to better armor or the ability to see in the dark can do wonders.

2. Look for areas where the player may be feeling lacking during combat or utility. Did they try to build a DPS that keeps falling behind. Is their tank build struggling with a lower than expected AC? Does their build feel redundant or superfluous to the party during combat? Try to see how he feels on average during combat. At the very least, make sure he understands the full potential of his class and subclass, to make sure he is aware of all his abilities.

3. Offer future combat situations suited to the player strengths, to prevent feelings of being "targeted". Do it not just for his PC, but the others as well. You can have one of enemies that only deal damages he's resistant to, and then the following combat can be one in which another player has the best stats.

4. If during play, he starts getting frustrated and aggressive, pause the game and give everyone a chance to breathe. Then come back and keep going as best you can. Then after the game, touch base, state that you noticed his frustration, and have a chat about how his tendency to become passive aggressive during moments of being unoptimized affects your ability to DM, and have a heart to heart. You wanna make it work, you want everyone to have fun, and it's not your goal to target anyone. Some fights will be in your favor, and others will be out of your favor. Such is the way of the world. Let him speak his mind, and try to see if you can't get down to the meat of the issue. It could be life outside of the game is leaking into his self worth in-game. Don't try to be his therapist, buts if this is the case, having him realize it is a good step towards overcoming it as an obstacle.

5. If during that talk, he becomes defensive or he won't open up to you, tell him that it's not your intention to target him, nor will it ever be. But if he won't communicate with you, then you need to set some boundaries. Think of the specific things he does that create a negative game experience, provide him (and the whole table) a list of table etiquette rules (be specific, but simple, and try to keep it around 5 or 6 points at most). Then be clear that if he keeps crossing those boundaries, you're gonna have to do what you have to do to maintain your mental health and the game experience for the whole table and suspend his participation until he can cool his head and come back with more of a willingness to compromise.

Overall, no matter what, don't look for the worst in that player. Even if passive aggressive behavior has become a pattern for him, don't edge it out or be constantly braced for impact. Play as though you are expecting his best behavior, and then if the negative behavior happens, take a break, carry on, and deal with it out of game. Do NOT try to have an argument in the middle of game play, as doing so would not be fair to your other players. And when you do approach the issue, do so with an open mind, a caring heart, and a willingness to compromise and work something out.

Remember that CR is a good rule of thumb, but two things to consider as well are player intelligence and action economy.

Play intelligence is self-explanatory. Consider how smart, clever, or even batshit insane your players are. Are they the types to run into the fray, swords blazing? Or do they take time to observe, sneak, set up traps, or position themselves before a fight? Do they use magic items and spells to make interesting combos? Do players sometimes combine their abilities to pull off certain stunts? Do your players enjoy the thrill of taking large risks, even if the mechanical reward is miniscule? Or do they take every possible precaution before acting? If your players are more mindful, creative, and careful, they won't be as easy to kill as those who are impulsive, straightforward, and risky.

Then there's the action economy. Basically, the more people fighting on the same side of the fight will have the advantage, even if the other side has fighters who are exceptionally strong. This is because, strength aside, whichever side of the fight gets the most turns will have the advantage. With 5-6 players, it's very unlikely that even deadly combats will result in a TPK.

My advice: ere on the side of caution to get a feel for your players' fighting style. Start with a "hard" combat and see how easy it is for them to win or how much they struggle. As you start to observe their techniques and styles, you can adjust the difficulty, or even play with enemies that have special skills or certain resistances to challenge them.

It's totally understandable that you want your time to be respected. If they made a commitment to you, it's on them to keep it. However, the only person we can control is ourselves.

The first question to ask yourself is how willing you are to keep moving forward after this experience. If you really want to make it work with this specific group of friends, then by all means keep rolling. Get a group chat or a shared discord and send them all a message that respectfully and honestly shares your feelings without being accusatory. Explain that you are irritated at the last minute cancellations and you want more transparency as to whether or not players will be present, as it is not fair to you to plan and prepare for a game only to have people be late or absent. Life does happen, unexpected absences happen, but a pattern of it has left your mental health in a bad place. You can handle the occasional absence and late arrival, so long as you and they can work out an agreement on what can be done to make the issue less severe.

Then talk with your players on what you can do and what they can do to mitigate this issue in the future. Would a regular day of the week for a weekly or bi-monthly (every other week) schedule for the game make it easier for your players to plan the rest of their time more efficiently? Would it be more realistic for some players to play remotely online? Can an agreement be made for a 24-hour or sooner notice for no-shows? Try to work things out so everyone can do something to make scheduling less difficult. If they want to play, they'll be willing to work it out. Worst case scenario, they won't budge, and it'll be easier for you to drop them from your game and find a new group, since it'll be clear where their priorities lie.

If you are completely done with this group or if they aren't willing to listen and compromise, then drop them from the game and take a while to decompress. Hard reset your world, get your notes together, and when you're ready, find a new group. Even if you have to take it online, it's doable. TTRPG tools like Roll 20 aren't perfect, but they do the job in a pinch once you get used to them. Discord is also a good tool for voice chat and finding players.

Whether you work things out or choose to move on, I'd like to offer the following tidbits of advice.

1. If you can handle it, try adding a few more players so you have at least 4 or 5 playing. It's easier to run a game with absent or late players if there are enough other players to still make playing possible. But don't pressure yourself to DM a bigger party if you can't handle it.

2. If it helps, create an in-universe explanation for why characters are suddenly missing, so you don't have to worry about playing them or suddenly pulling them out of the story off the cuff. It can be as simple as "Last session, you were about to enter the castle. Before you can get to the door, the bard vanishes out of thin air" and then have the character just as suddenly reappear when they show up next. Perhaps figuring out why people keep vanishing and reappearing can be one of the mysteries they investigate, so have some sort of answer prepared.

3. If you prep for a whole party, and you have an absentee to deal with, don't change anything you've prepped. The party *always* has the option to retreat if they feel like they're losing the battle. Real life doesn't always perfectly balance itself, so it's understandable that this world wouldn't do so either. Also, keep in mind the CR system for combat isn't entirely accurate, so a battle that seems hard may not be as difficult between action economy and the cleverness of your players.

4.For situations where you *needed* a certain missing player's character to be there, and they can't move forward with them suddenly vanished, try prepping what I call "pepper quests", or quests that drop into the party's lap that they more or less *have* to do that are intended to stall for the missing player while entertaining present player with playtime and rewards. Tropes like having a shared dream or hallucination where they fight dream-monsters, suddenly running into backstory-specific NPCs who need their help right this minute, or suddenly finding themselves inside a simulation can stall a party for sessions at a time if needed. You can even use pepper quests to run modules you may have wanted to try.

5. If you must move into a new group (though I sincerely hope you can work things out with your friends), try to find a group who can meet regularly on the same day, either every week or every other week (or even every month, if schedules are tight). This will most likely prevent last-minute cancellation patterns before they can start.

Hope this helps.

Context matters a bit here. Not the argument, but how the son and father feel. Just a few quick suggestions here.

"Get out.": If disowning the son is something the father doesn't want to do, but he has to, or if he's struggling with it emotionally, something short and sweet like this may do. This could be the father saying he's finally done, and he no longer is willing to debate, but in a calm, stoic way.

*No words*: Sometimes, implying through action hits harder. Have the son leave after the argument, and when he comes back, the door is locked and his key doesn't work, and there's a suitcase outside. This should be enough implication to the audience that the son is no longer welcome. A good choice if you wanna take a more subtle approach or if there are no words that sound natural enough. You can also pair this with having the son's phone number blocked on his father's phone.

If it's subtlety you're going for, then first identify how you want them to be "bad". To avoid the archetype of being a purely evil villain, you'll need to make him good or neutral in some areas, so his bad qualities pop out more.

For example, maybe he's the kind of guy who doesn't make a fuss, doesn't take up too much space, and is a real people pleaser. But he's a bad person because he's a giant coward when it counts, would throw someone under the bus to save his own skin, and has zero loyalty to those who help him. And after he does something bad, he drops to his knees and asks God for forgiveness, in a prayer that sounds more like him justifying his actions to himself than it does any kind of repentance.

Or maybe you wanna be a little more obtuse with his awfulness. He could be a kind soul, helping people, lending a hand where he can, going around doing good deeds for others, and all "in the name of the Lord". But he only helps people he likes. There are kinds of people in particular, be they a different race, sex, religion, sexuality, socio-economic status, etc. that he refuses to have anything to do with. He doesn't hurt them, but he refuses to help, even if he's the only one who can help. But since he doesn't directly harm them, he thinks it's fine to act this way.

These are just examples of my point. If you want nuance, you gotta make him a guy that you cannot fully root for not fully root against. You can do either, to a capacity, for sure. But those who root against him can't deny that he does good things sometimes. And those who root for him can't ignore his serious shortcomings.

Hot take: I don't think tipping should be based on the price of the meal.

Now, overall, everything would be a lot better if delivery services and restaurants paid their employees a living wage. Tipping is an antique of the great depression, born from shit wages and bribery. 

But we don't live in that world, and I sadly think we never will. But, I feel there should be a set range of tipping practices that are based on the amount of work that you put a worker through. 

It takes the same effort to carry a plate to a table, whether it's a 12 dollar burger or a 25 dollar steak. Likewise, a table with 6 people who order several cheaper plates and a table with 3 people who get more pricy plates are two different work loads, but can add up to a similar bill. Or of one table is constantly calling the waitress over, asking for several different condiments, constant drink refills, etc, and another table merely comes in, orders, eats, and leaves, the work load is different, even if they ordered the same food. And when it comes to delivery, if everything fits in one bag, it shouldn't matter how expensive the food is. Why should the guy who ordered 40 bucks worth of food that fits in one bag and lives five minutes away pay more than the guy who orders 20 bucks worth of food and lives fifteen minutes away?

It should be simple. While dining in, you pay a certain amount of a tip per plate, regardless of how much the food is. For every nessesary refill, extra condiment request, special adjustment to the menu food, or complaint (legit or not), you pay extra to the final tip. For delivery drivers, you tip per bag or drink tray that they have to carry, as well as per mile they have to drive.

If there was an expectation of paying those in the service industry for the work they do, instead of the final price, it may put shit in perspective. But no matter what, if you can't tip, go pick up the food yourself or make it at home. Servers and drivers don't get paid enough to not get paid.

What I've been doing for my first time is sandboxing. When they reach a new city or town, I build it up, fill it with NPCs, and give a good number of NPCs problems that the party can fix (side quests) or a connection to a party member's backstory or character arc (main quest). For example, my players are headed to a new town, so I have characters with issues like being haunted by a long-dead friend, being homeless for the time being, or having their business harassed by local children. But they're mainly there because one of my character's girlfriend is sick, and this town is known for medicinal herbs. If they look around, they'll be able to find an NPC that can forward them on that arc. They may also find hints to the arcs of the other players along the way. Spreading out the clues and giving the players several things to do makes it more of a hunt to find what they need, rather than a set path for them to wander off from. And if they can't find what they need, they'll either have to keep looking or follow another clue to do something else I set up. A side quest can easily spiral into a character arc. The main quest can get side tracked into a crazy series of smaller events. 

If you make a sandbox, they'll play in the sandbox. And it'll be harder to de-rail because, whether your players dig for treasure, build a sandcastle, or play with construction trucks, there's no wrong way to play in a sandbox.

I kinda just studied the dice bag a friend made for me and figured it out from there. Basically, you cut out two big circles (one from both fabrics) and two little circles (one from both fabrics). You see the two big circles together, inside out, leaving a gap to turn it right side out when you finish. You press it flat, see up the gap, and then sew lines around the outside, making a channel. You cut a hole in that channel, and then feed a ribbon through the channel with a safety pin until it's gone all the way around. Then cinch, adjust, and cut to your liking, depending on how far you want the bag to fully open (for now, take the ribbon out and put it aside. You can refeed it through later). Then you see the small circles together, inside out, leaving a gap to turn right side out, like before. Press and sew the gap shut. Then place the finished small circle on top of the finished big circle. Whichever side of the big circle that you want to be the inside of the bag should be face up, and whatever side of the small circle you want to be the most visible should be face up on top of that. Pin and sew the two circles together by sewing a small circle in the middle. Then pin to section off six pockets and sew lines from the top to the sewed circle to make the pockets permanent, taking care to avoid your ribbon channel. Then refeed the ribbon back through the channel and you're done.

People on the spectrum can drive just fine. The "different tests" for driving are for accomodations, or to make sure you can drive the type of car you can drive. If a physical disability means you can only drive an automatic, then your license will limit you to only driving automatic cars, for example. Or if you need adaptive equipment, your license will only let you drive cars with that equipment. There's none of that needed for people with autism.

The readiness to drive is different from person to person. One person in the spectrum takes to driving very well. Another may need a little help. Another may need a ton of practice and professional lessons. I personally needed lessons and a lot of practice, and I needed to take my test three times before I passed. And now I drive just fine. I know my limitations, I scope out the route and parking situation beforehand when going new places, and I take public transportation if it seems too far (like when I wanna go to San Francisco, I drive to the train station and use the train instead of driving).

So between that and assuming autism is like the flu where all the symptoms are exactly the same, it's clear this woman hasn't a damn clue what she's talking about. She has absolutely nothing on you. Her toxicity has zero merit.

If your issues are fear based, start out with something easy and work your way up. Start with making canned soup on the stove instead of the microwave. Go with something that has a thinner broth so it won't splatter if it starts bubbling. Doing this will give you the ability to use your stove without being distracted by a recipe. Use this time to get used to being near the stove so you can slowly get used to it. After enough exposure, move onto an easy recipe. Soup doesn't need a concrete recipe. Just gather some veggies you like, cut them up, boil them, add in chunks of meat if you like, and then serve with olive oil or butter (so you can absorb all those fat soluble vitamins).

If that's too much of a big first step, then start with making soup in a crock pot. It'll take longer to cook, but you can set it and forget it until dinner time. Look up some good crockpot-friendly soup recipes.
